question.problem: If ${f}^{′}(x)=-|x+1|,$ which of the following could be the graph of a continuous function $y=f(x)?$
question.worked_solution:
The graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$ is the following:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/c4e03ef210691e4eee922d0c35e90abb9cde1a78064ad491d4ac084d875c4a57.png)

Recall that critical points of $y=f(x)$ occur when ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(x)$ does not exist. In our case, there is one critical point: 

$\,$ $x=-1$ 

Also, we have the following: 

- If ${f}^{′}(x)>0$ then $f(x)$ is increasing.

- If ${f}^{′}(x)<0$ then $f(x)$ is decreasing.

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below.

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,-1)$ | $-1$ | $(-1,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${f}^{′}$ | $-$ | $0$ | $-$ |
| $f$ | $↘$ | $\text{no extr.}$ | $↘$ |

Let's now sketch the graph of $y=f(x):$

- First, we draw the critical point. We choose an arbitrary point on the vertical line $x=-1,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/40b5e9b8928be63a415877c0633f0302c874db51b1c74a1f82b7b1526a6f4d14.png)

- Next, we consider the behavior of $y=f(x)$ in the neighborhood of the critical points:

- Since $f(x)$ is decreasing $↘$ on $(-\infty ,-1)$ and is decreasing $↘$ on $(-1,\infty )$, the graph of $y=f(x)$ goes up to the left of $x=-1$ and goes down to the right of $x=-1.$

- Furthermore, since ${f}^{′}(x)$ is increasing to the left of $x=-1$, we must have ${f}^{″}(x)>0$, and, since it is decreasing to the right of $x=-1$, we must have ${f}^{″}(x)<0.$ So, $x=-1$ is an inflection point at which the curve $y=f(x)$ changes from concave up to concave down.

So, we can draw as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/c68544957f33afdeab436a3fbf75b9e27990a2e7f3ea75f39c6e58dce24f6185.png)

 

- Finally, since we are told that our graph must be continuous, by connecting and extending the existing parts with a smooth curve, we obtain a possible graph of $y=f(x):$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/4c91ba8f06642fe14035400efa61dbd2d8bbadd07274fedc9a90678970bbb9a8.png)

 

**Note:** The graph we obtained is not the only possible one. Any similar graph that's shifted vertically up or down could also be considered a possible $y=f(x).$
